title: ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Sets Stephanie March to Return as Alexandra Cabot
description:
Assistant district attorney Alexandra Cabot is back.

	Stephanie March will appear in the ninth episode of “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” Seas
body:
Assistant district attorney Alexandra Cabot is back.

	Stephanie March will appear in the ninth episode of “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” Season 28 to reprise the role she has played in more than 100 episodes. March was a member of the main “Special Victims Unit” cast from Season 2 in 2000 to Season 5 in 2003, when Cabot had to fake her own death and enter a witness protection program. She has returned to the series as a guest several times over the years across Seasons 6, 10, 11, 13 and most recently Season 19 in 2018. She also played Cabot in the 2006 legal drama “Conviction,” a short-lived “SVU” spinoff.
	

	Besides “SVU,” March’s prominent credits include Ricky Gervais’ 2009 comedy film “The Invention of Lying,” Matthew Newton’s 2017 indie film “Who We Are Now,” Laura Kosann 2019 mockumentary “The Social Ones” and Ava Duvernay’s 2023 film “Origin.” She also collaborated with Duvernay on her 2022 series “Naomi.” In 2023, she was in the Amazon Prime Video series “Harlan Coben’s Shelter.” She is repped by Paradigm and Navigation Media Group.


	Created by Dick Wolf, “SVU” is the longest-running primetime drama in the history of American Television. The series airs on Thursdays at 9 p.m. The current cast includes Mariska Hargitay, Ice T, Peter Scanavino, Kelli Giddish, Kevin Kane, Aimé Donna Kelly and Corey Cott. Wolf executive produces alongside Hargitay, Michele Fazekas, Kenneth Brown, Rebecca McGill, Anastasia Puglisi and Peter Jankowski. Universal Television produces the series in association with Wolf Entertainment.

schema.headline: ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Sets Stephanie March to Return as Alexandra Cabot

title: Sandra Hüller Joins ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ in Cameo Role
description:
Oscar nominee Sandra Hüller will make a cameo in Marvel’s “Avengers: Doomsday.”

	News of Hüller’s top-secret role comes as directors Anthony and J
body:
Oscar nominee Sandra Hüller will make a cameo in Marvel’s “Avengers: Doomsday.”

	News of Hüller’s top-secret role comes as directors Anthony and Joe Russo are in post-production on the project, ahead of its Dec. 18 release date. The superhero movie is already stuffed to the gills with award-winning actors and massive movie stars, including Chris Hemsworth, Pedro Pascal, Paul Rudd, Anthony Mackie, Florence Pugh, Vanessa Kirby, Patrick Stewart, Ian McKellen, Tom Hiddleston and Channing Tatum, plus more “Black Panther,” “Thunderbolts,” “Fantastic Four” and “X-Men” actors. The movie also features the much-anticipated returns of Chris Evans as Steve Rogers and Oscar winner Robert Downey Jr. as Victor von Doom, taking on the villainous role instead of Iron Man/Tony Stark.
	

	Not much has been revealed about the plot for “Avengers: Doomsday,” except for the fact that Downey’s Doctor Doom represents the superheroes’ most dangerous foe yet. Rumors about Hüller’s involvement began swirling a couple of weeks ago, with some fans speculating she could be tied to Downey’s Doom (perhaps his mother) or that she might play another of the Latverian Witches (who don the colorful robes Marvel displayed at this year’s Comic-Con).


	The Marvel cameo also marks Hüller’s fifth major feature in 2026, following “Project Hail Mary” (with newly announced Marvel superhero Ryan Gosling, who’ll play Ghost Rider), “Rose,” “Fatherland” and “Digger,” all of which are players in this year’s awards race. In 2024, the German star  earned her first best actress Oscar nomination for “Anatomy of a Fall,” one of two best picture nominees in which she starred that year. (The other film was “The Zone of Interest,” which won two Oscars, including best international feature; “Anatomy of a Fall” won the Oscar for best original screenplay.)
	

	The Hollywood Reporter first reported Hüller’s involvement. Marvel Studios does not comment on casting.

schema.headline: Sandra Hüller Joins ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ in Cameo Role

title: Ethan Klein Reacts to Hila Klein’s Cheating Allegations Amid ‘H3 Podcast’ Fallout: ‘Please Respect My Family’s Privacy … They Have Nothing to Do With This’
description: Ethan Klein has spoken out after the implosion of his marriage and the “H3 Podcast” due to cheating allegations from his wife, Hila Klein, who publ
body:
Ethan Klein has spoken out after the implosion of his marriage and the “H3 Podcast” due to cheating allegations from his wife, Hila Klein, who publicly accused him of having a six-month romantic affair.

	“I know a lot of people are understandably looking for a comment from me, but I ask that you please respect my family’s privacy and do not contact them looking for me or asking for their comments,” Klein wrote in an Instagram Story on Friday. “They have nothing to do with this and share in your outrage and disappointment. Thank you.”
	

	After meeting in 2007, Ethan and Hila built their YouTube careers together and got married in 2012. The Los Angeles-based couple have three children together. They launched the “H3 Podcast” in 2016. On YouTube, it currently has 2.5 million subscribers.


	In response to the cheating allegations, the podcast production crew  sided with Hila and unanimously agreed that they would cut ties with Ethan.

	In an Instagram post late Thursday night, Hila wrote, “I am living a nightmare I can’t wake up from. My husband has been having an affair. I have been fed lie after lie after lie for months. Here is the truth.”

	She continued: “I could sense something was wrong. I tried to ask him questions and share my concerns and hurt feelings. But I was met with dismissive answers and no action. Things that bothered me continued to bother me, and he did nothing about it. So I trusted him. Because I loved him. I stopped questioning him and began to question myself, my own instincts. My sanity.”According to Hila Klein, “Eventually, he was caught in a lie, and I knew I was done. But the lies continued. ‘It was just a kiss’ became ‘it was emotional cheating.’ After I dragged these lies from him, he finally admitted he’d been in an affair for over 6 months, the extent of which I’m sure I still don’t know.”

	“The betrayal I feel is immeasurable. The person I loved and trusted for 20 years evaporated overnight. He was my safe place, my partner in marriage, parenting, and business,” Hila wrote. “My only family on this side of the world. How do I even begin to make sense of this?”
	

	She concluded, “I don’t know what comes next; I’ve never been here before. I am in survival mode, trying to navigate separation, co-parenting, and unthinkable heartbreak. All I can do right now is focus on taking care of myself and my children, one day at a time. You’re not crazy. Trust your instincts. Trust yourself. If you’re not being treated right, get up and leave.”

	The “H3” crew, in a statement posted on Instagram, said, “We stand with Hila and will support her every step of the way. We’re disgusted by Ethan’s actions and the hurt he has caused. We all deserved better: Hila, us, and you.”

	“We are all shocked, angry, and heartbroken to learn about Ethan’s ongoing affair,” the H3 team said. “As soon as we found out, we all agreed: we would not continue working with Ethan involved or profiting in any way. We don’t yet know what that means for the future. There’s a lot to work through, and we wish we had more answers for you.”

	The “H3 Podcast” crew’s statement concluded, “Please know that we’re safe, we’re sticking together, and we’re looking after each other. We’ve put so much of ourselves into this show, and it’s hard to find the words for what we’re feeling right now. Thank you for giving us some time to figure things out, and for all the love you’ve shown us. We love you, and we miss you already.”

schema.headline: Ethan Klein Reacts to Hila Klein’s Cheating Allegations Amid ‘H3 Podcast’ Fallout: ‘Please Respect My Family’s Privacy … They Have Nothing to Do With This’

title: Zendaya Sets ‘Dune 3’ Oscar Campaign for Best Actress in Category Shake-Up (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Zendaya is “Dune’s” leading lady.

	Multiple sources tell Variety that Zendaya will campaign for Oscar consideration in the lead actress category f
body:
Zendaya is “Dune’s” leading lady.

	Multiple sources tell Variety that Zendaya will campaign for Oscar consideration in the lead actress category for her role as Chani in “Dune: Part Three,” the final chapter of Denis Villeneuve’s sci-fi epic. The move marks a shift from the first two films, where she was positioned in supporting actress.

	Warner Bros. and representatives for Zendaya declined to comment.


	The decision reflects Chani’s expanded role in the story. “Dune: Part Three” is set nearly two decades after Paul Atreides (Timothée Chalamet) seized control of the Imperium. Now a ruthless emperor, Paul must face the consequences of his reign as old allies return, terrifying new threats emerge and betrayal lurks in every shadow. Haunted by visions of imperial collapse and the reappearance of his long-lost love, Paul is drawn into a sweeping conspiracy, with Chani at the heart of its unfolding mystery. As rebellion brews and enemies close in, Paul must confront the true cost of power and the fate of those he loves most. The film also stars Jason Momoa, Florence Pugh, Rebecca Ferguson, Anya Taylor-Joy, Robert Pattinson, Javier Bardem, Josh Brolin, Charlotte Rampling and Isaach de Bankolé.
	

	The film caps a stellar year for the 30-year-old multi-hyphenate, who could find herself in contention across multiple categories and films this season.

	She kicked off 2026 starring as Emma Harwood, a literary editor who reveals shocking secrets, in the romantic dark comedy “The Drama” from writer-director Kristoffer Borgli. That performance, opposite Robert Pattinson, will also be submitted in lead.
	

	She followed it with her turn as Athena in Christopher Nolan’s billion-dollar mythological adaptation “The Odyssey,” where she will vie for supporting actress recognition alongside co-stars Anne Hathaway, Samantha Morton and Charlize Theron.

	She also reprised her role as MJ in Destin Daniel Cretton’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” another billion-dollar hit that now ranks among the highest-grossing films of all time.

	Zendaya’s relatively brief career has already produced an impressive haul of hardware. She won two Emmys for her role as Rue in the HBO Max drama “Euphoria,” becoming the youngest two-time winner in the lead drama actress category. She picked up a Golden Globe in 2023 for the same role. In 2025, she earned two Golden Globe nominations for Luca Guadagnino’s tennis romance “Challengers,” one for lead actress in a comedy and another as a producer when the film was nominated for best picture (musical or comedy).

	An Oscar nomination this year would be her first.

	Warner Bros. will release “Dune: Part Three” in theaters and Imax on Dec. 18.

schema.headline: Zendaya Sets ‘Dune 3’ Oscar Campaign for Best Actress in Category Shake-Up (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Sacha Baron Cohen Says Donald Trump Has ‘Elements of Brilliance’ and ‘We Were Too Easy to Dismiss Him as a Nincompoop’
description: 20 years after retiring Ali G, Sacha Baron Cohen has dusted off his tracksuit collection and reprised the character for “Ali G: Who Iz I?,” now ope
body:
20 years after retiring Ali G, Sacha Baron Cohen has dusted off his tracksuit collection and reprised the character for “Ali G: Who Iz I?,” now open in theaters before coming to Amazon Prime Oct. 30. The comedian first brought Ali G to audiences at the turn of the century with “Da Ali G Show,” where he interviewed some of the world’s most powerful figures (and, more often than not, made fools of them in the process).

	“As Ali G, I had the privilege of sitting with some of the smartest and most powerful people in the world, and all of them were punctual,” Baron Cohen told Josh Horowitz Wednesday night during a live taping of “Happy Sad Confused” at New York’s 92nd Street Y. After a lengthy pause, he turned his attention to the one exception: “Donald Trump kept us waiting for about 40 minutes.”
	

	Baron Cohen recalled feeling “intimidated” upon entering Trump Tower with director James Bobin, where they waited in a room while Trump shouted a string of expletives “not for the likes of delicate Jewish ears” at Rudy Giuliani over the phone.


	“Later on, I heard that he used to do that with other people,” Baron Cohen said. “It really was a power move.”

	Trump appeared taken with Bobin, who Baron Cohen described as a “very handsome, blond, Oxford-educated” Englishman. But when he realized he’d be sitting down with Ali G instead, his demeanor “immediately” changed.

	“I actually met a woman who was in the car with him after that interview, and he was apparently furious,” Baron Cohen said. “He actually went out publicly a couple of times to criticize me. And in the end, we used all those clips and used them to advertise another show that I did.”
	

	Baron Cohen’s interview with Trump aired in 2003, back when the future president was best known as a New York real estate mogul, before going on to host NBC’s “The Apprentice.” Looking back at their encounter, Baron Cohen said he could understand how Trump won a second term in the White House, pointing to the president’s “elements of brilliance.”

	“I mean, how has he survived a second term? People underestimated him,” Baron Cohen said. “We were too easy to dismiss him as a nincompoop. There are elements of brilliance to him, otherwise. And that explains his appeal with the fact that he’s there for a second term, the fact that he’s transforming this country. I won’t say positively or negatively.”

	This was not the only time Baron Cohen reflected on Trump’s one-of-a-kind characteristics on his latest press tour. He told Kara Swisher and Scott Galloway on the Pivot podcast that the president is “amusing” and that there’s “a huge amount of comedy in the way he speaks.”

	“He’s intentionally being funny,” Baron Cohen explained. “And if you have a look on the far right, they use comedy and sarcasm as an engaging way to dismiss criticisms.”

	Baron Cohen suggests that Trump’s popularity, perhaps, reflects a broader theme explored through his own collection of provocative characters: “In the black and white, the world is a little bit complicated.”

schema.headline: Sacha Baron Cohen Says Donald Trump Has ‘Elements of Brilliance’ and ‘We Were Too Easy to Dismiss Him as a Nincompoop’

title: El Gouna’s CineGouna Expands Industry Push: ‘We Want to Give Every Filmmaker a Chance’
description: More than 320 Arab film projects applied to CineGouna Funding this year, including more than 100 from Egypt, as the industry arm of Egypt’s El Goun
body:
More than 320 Arab film projects applied to CineGouna Funding this year, including more than 100 from Egypt, as the industry arm of Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival drew submissions from across the region. At the festival’s ninth edition, running through Oct. 23 on the Red Sea, CineGouna is adding new initiatives as it looks to fill gaps in the regional film landscape.

	The volume of Egyptian submissions alone prompted El Gouna to create Egyptian Voices, a new strand giving four additional local projects training in pitching, packaging and co-production.
	

	“There are three big gaps in the Arab world,” Ahmed Shawky, who heads CineGouna Funding, tells Variety, pointing to the lack of national film funds in many countries, limited co-production treaties and the volatility of regional funding.

	Shawky, a film critic and festival programmer, points to Egypt, where the film commission focuses on attracting foreign productions rather than financing local films. “In Egypt, we don’t have a national film fund, with 100 years of cinema history, more than 4,000 features,” he notes.

	Regional funds have helped fill some of that void, but Shawky says their resources can fluctuate, leaving filmmakers uncertain about available support.

	At El Gouna this week, CineGouna Funding awarded more than $350,000 in cash and services, with 40 awards going to 16 of the 19 participating projects. Syrian filmmaker Rama Abdy’s documentary “House No. 7,” about three women building a refuge in Damascus, won the $15,000 CineGouna Platform Award for a project in post-production. Algerian filmmaker Zoulikha Tahar’s “Paradise Beach,” previously selected for Berlinale Talents, took the $15,000 award for a project in development.
	

	Sudanese filmmaker Marwa Zein’s “Lily’s Makkah,” her first fiction feature after the documentary “Khartoum Offside,” received a €10,000 grant, post-production support and an invitation to Durban FilmMart. The participating projects also held more than 140 one-on-one meetings with companies, institutions and international festivals.

	CineGouna’s work extends beyond financing. CineGouna Emerge, its program for emerging filmmakers and film professionals from Egypt, the Arab world and Africa, focuses on access.

	Egyptian filmmaker, producer and programmer Hayat Aljowaily, who heads Emerge, recalls that the program initially focused on covering the costs of bringing participants to El Gouna. But getting newcomers through the door did not necessarily give them the confidence or connections to navigate a film festival.

	“Year after year, we realized that access alone wasn’t enough, and that we had to create an environment and carve out a space for these participants,” she explains. “It’s about creating a community,” she goes on.

	Emerge has since added mentorship, workshops, industry meetings and a dedicated “campus” in the heart of the festival. More than 300 participants have passed through the program, with this year’s cohort spanning 16 nationalities and including Egyptians from 20 of the country’s 27 governorates.

	For Aljowaily, that geographic reach is central to Emerge’s purpose. “It’s not just for Cairo, but also for other cities,” she says, noting that El Gouna “is not really accessible for all Egypt.”

	Aljowaily points to a young woman from Upper Egypt who came to El Gouna last year having never been to a cinema. Selected from around 1,000 applicants, she pitched a project that was picked up by an Egyptian short-film producer and received one of two university scholarships, allowing her to move to Cairo to study cinema.

	Other participants have moved between different parts of CineGouna. Jordanian filmmaker Asmahan Bakirat pitched as a director last year, returned this year as a producer and was selected for Emerge’s Rising Stars program.

	CineGouna Forum, headed by producer and screenwriter Ahmed Amer, brings filmmakers and industry figures together for panels, masterclasses and discussions.
	

	This year’s sessions included “Producing Against the Odds,” featuring Palestinian producer May Odeh, who has three films at the festival (“Safe Exit,” “Yesterday the Eye Didn’t Sleep,” “Dear Ajayi” and “Outside the Expected Frame”) with Toronto Film Festival programming director Robyn Citizen.

	Amer sees tighter financing as potentially pushing filmmakers toward lower budgets and different creative choices, including genre films. But money is not the only resource he thinks the region needs.

	“Filmmakers need more creative producers,” Amer stresses. “Funding is definitely an issue, but creative producers are needed badly.”

	“I often meet filmmakers and producers who are only thinking about their current projects,” Amer continues. “We often forget that we need to carefully plan a career. One film is a part of a longer journey.”

	For Shawky, financing can also influence the kinds of films that get made. He sees two currents among Arab filmmakers: those responding directly to war, political upheaval and social issues, and others pursuing more personal or genre-driven stories. International funds and markets often favor the former, he argues.

	“Only focusing on traumatizing topics makes filmmakers impose self-censorship,” Shawky contends. “Even if they have two topics, they will pick the one that sounds sexy for funders.”

	“We want to give every filmmaker a chance,” he adds. “And it’s up to the artist to decide whether to tackle those topics or simply make art.”

	Lebanese filmmaker Karim Kassem’s “Pipes,” which premiered in Karlovy Vary’s Crystal Globe competition, came through CineGouna Funding, where it won a Red Sea post-production award that helped complete its sound mix.

	“But it wasn’t only the award,” Kassem recalls. “The contacts I made here, before and after the pitch, were incredibly important to the journey of the film.”

	Moroccan filmmaker Yassine El Idrissi had a similar trajectory with “Halima,” which came to CineGouna in post-production before premiering in Shanghai’s main competition and winning best director and best actress. “CineGouna was the first platform we applied to,” he explains. “That gave us confidence in the project and helped make the film known.”
	

	Both filmmakers return to El Gouna this year with their completed films in competition, completing what Shawky describes as a “full circuit.”

	As El Gouna approaches its 10th edition, Shawky says the next step is strengthening CineGouna’s international presence and developing more year-round activity beyond the annual festival.

schema.headline: El Gouna’s CineGouna Expands Industry Push: ‘We Want to Give Every Filmmaker a Chance’

title: ‘The Cycle’ Is a Surprising New Take on the Police Procedural, With a Huge Twist and an Emotional Resonance the Director Didn’t Expect
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “The Cycle,” now streaming on Shudder.

	What if a werewolf continued to transform even aft
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “The Cycle,” now streaming on Shudder.

	What if a werewolf continued to transform even after its death?

	This light bulb idea came to frequent collaborators Jordan Downey and Kevin Stewart as they were sketching out a TV treatment for their 2018 film “The Head Hunter.”


	“We both looked at each other and stopped and were like, ‘Wait, that’s a really cool, fun idea and a take on werewolves that we’ve never seen before,’” Downey says. “Being the horror cinephiles that we are, we were like, ‘I don’t think anyone’s done that. I can’t think of a movie or a show.’ We Googled it and realized, no, it hasn’t been done. What do you do with that idea?”
	

	The result is “The Cycle,” a handsomely shot detective story following Meg (Deborah Ann Woll) and Marks (Jeffrey Donovan) as experts trying to solve a lycanthropic murder mystery — although the film largely keeps the exact supernatural entity a mystery, until the third act goes full creature feature.

	Downey, who co-wrote the film with Stewart and directed it, thought that outsized hook would benefit from a recognizable framing.

	“Right away, it felt like it fit best into a crime mystery, a police procedural,” he says. “Ultimately, if you have this werewolf that is going to reanimate and then at dawn turn back into a man — but in this case it’s a deceased man who doesn’t move, walk, talk, has no life — that would just be dumbfounding to police. They would come into this crime scene and they would see these victims, but then they’d find this naked dead guy not knowing that he’s harboring something supernatural. So it made sense that there really wasn’t another package to put it into.”
	



	

					“The Cycle”
									©AMC/courtesy Everett Collection
	



	Once the case is cracked, the third act shifts hard into monster movie mode, complete with plenty of practical blood, guts and werewolf nastiness.

	“I love creature features,” Downey says. “I didn’t want it to be this ‘elevated,’ pretentious experience that didn’t give monster movie fans the proper experience. You go into ‘The Cycle’ not knowing that’s what’s coming. I thought what would happen is the characters would be thrust into a completely crazy change in their lives, that they now exist in a world where werewolves can be real and there’s one in proximity to them. That change would be as shocking to them as it hopefully would be to the audience. So we were aware of trying to do things early in the movie, so when that tonal shift happens, it felt earned but also surprising.”

	Ushering in the change of pace was the transformation scene, which is one of the most loved traditions in werewolf movies and was exciting for the team to plan for, along with key special effects artist and supervisor Patrick Magee.

	“The first thing was acknowledging that if you’re going to make a werewolf movie, we didn’t want to run from that challenge,” Downey says. “In the ’80s, Rob Bottin and Rick Baker nailed it with ‘The Howling’ and ‘An American Werewolf in London.’ In the years since, people have shied away from it because either it’s too expensive, too time-consuming or maybe there’s a clever new way of doing it. But we just felt like enough time had gone where we hadn’t seen that done very well for so many years. So we said right away, ‘If we’re going to do this, we have to do a proper werewolf transformation. We have to nail it.’ We storyboarded it a lot. We talked about it a lot. We broke down the best scenes that had been done and thought about … Do we want to see foot? Do we want to see hands? Do we want to see eyes, teeth? Is it a spinal cord? All of the different things that we wanted to see in our scene, and then how it would apply to an undead corpse version of a transformation.
	

	Beyond the horror element, the film examines the complex choices that can come with fatherhood, which comes most notably via Meg, who learns that her long-lost parent is the werewolf at the heart of the story.

	“It wasn’t in the first drafts, to be honest,” Downey says. “In our initial treatments, Meg was investigating a stranger. It was the same concept that a man’s body was discovered, the police didn’t know how he was tied to these murders, and they went to her because she was an expert in her field, but he wasn’t her father. We got her into Act Three, when she went to the house, just like in the movie where they go to investigate his whereabouts and the life of the recluse. We felt like she was putting herself in this really dangerous position, without some kind of an emotional tie to that character. I told Kevin that I don’t believe that the character would do this given the circumstances. We were also missing something that I thought is really important in horror films, which is the heart and the pathos of a monster movie and the tragedy. So then, we came up with the idea that, ‘OK, what if this is her father?’ So now we’ve anchored something to her emotionally. We can work in the tragedy of this man who left, but it was in her mind for a terrible reason, a father walking out on their children. In his mind, it was to protect them. And once we had that for her father, then we started to apply that theme to some of the other characters.”

	Much like the cycle of undead werewolves, it’s easy to see this story carry on through new chapters. Downey says he’s happy keeping “The Cycle” as a single story, but has also mulled over what a larger scope could be.
	

	“I think this movie is self-contained and there’s versions of it that I would probably not be interested in,” Downey says. “But we did talk a lot about different stories. I think there’s a great prequel in the original werewolf that came from over the sea. There’s an aquatic, boat-set version of this story that I think would be interesting. You could do a TV series about the life and the trials of [Meg’s father] Peter Stump and all of the different things that he was doing while isolated for those 30 years. I think it’d be interesting to see … because she’s so good at her job, and in the final scene of the movie so confident that she’s gonna get this figured out. But what if she didn’t? What if 10, 15, 20 years goes by and she has not solved it and she is now facing the same dilemma her dad was, which was, ‘This fucking thing can’t be stopped.’ But by killing herself, that does nothing. Finding her at a point of quit would be really interesting. I’d only want to do stuff if Deborah and Jeffrey wanted to come back and work on it again, and if there were fans that wanted it to happen, but I would never say no.”

	Watch the trailer for “The Cycle” below.

schema.headline: ‘The Cycle’ Is a Surprising New Take on the Police Procedural, With a Huge Twist and an Emotional Resonance the Director Didn’t Expect

title: Why Olivia Colman Didn’t Get Splinters From Getting Intimate With Alexander Skarsgård’s ‘Wicker’ Costume
description:
Believe the hype. “Wicker,” now in theaters, is every bit as horny, romantic and wonderful as the trailer leads you to believe.

	Olivia Colman pla
body:
Believe the hype. “Wicker,” now in theaters, is every bit as horny, romantic and wonderful as the trailer leads you to believe.

	Olivia Colman plays a spinster fisherwoman in a medieval community where marriage is what gives a woman worth. Although she is a fierce independent woman, the village mocks her as she goes about making her living. One day she goes to the local basket weaver, played by Peter Dinklage, and asks him to make her a wicker husband.
	

	Enter Alexander Skarsgård — yes, that is him under all that makeup — wearing a practical suit and prosthetic makeup to transform him into a basket man.


	It began with Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson, who were adapting Ursula Wills’ short story “The Wicker Husband.” Weta Workshop artists, prosthetic makeup designer Joe Dunckley and lead makeup FX artist Sarah Rubano received the script and a call from the writers and directors who told them, “We want to make this practically,” says Dunckley. “They wanted a piece of beautiful concept art that showed their vision.”

	The pair spent 18 months in research and development alone. Because prosthetic makeup materials are manufactured to imitate human flesh and skin, it posed a challenge. “This guy is made of wicker, so we had to do it a different way,” Dunckley says. He continues, “We tested our theory. We thought that if we could get the strands of the weave to be individual and get them to move as if they were individual muscle fibers that drove his movement, then he could be a believable sentient wicker being.”

	But they couldn’t mold it, so the pair were pushed toward modern innovation using 3D digital sculpting and 3D printing.
	

	They began with a full-body scan of Skarsgård so they could sculpt pieces specific to him.

	The intricate basket weave was created using a relatively new powder-bed laser-sintered printing process. Dunckley explains, “It’s a volume of thermoplastic elastomer; you shoot a laser into it and where that focal point of the laser is, it fuses the powder and you can build intricate weave and complex geometry. The powder in the bed holds the strands apart while they set.”

	And why didn’t Colman get splinters during the film’s steamy bonking scenes?

	Nearly all of Skarsgård’s costume was made up of 50 individual 3D-printed appliances that were painted to look like wicker before being stitched onto a suit made out of soft, flexible spandex — so no actual straw was involved.

	Dunckley says, “It’s a semiflexible material, not too dissimilar to the feeling of touching proper wicker weave.”



	

	



	As for the prosthetics, Rubano focused on the makeup, which comprised 10 individual pieces.

	Rubano says, “He would get into this very fitted suit and we would bounce between the makeup chair and getting him ready in the suit, depending on the different stages.” She goes on to say, “We had ears, eye bags and lips. We had an underlip piece and a jaw piece, and the larger forehead, nose, cheekbones and there was lots of hand painting around his eyes.”

	His facial hair — beard, hair and eyelashes — was constructed from muka, a silky-soft fiber extracted from the harakeke plant. This material allowed them to knot the individual strands onto the weave itself so they could cut and style it like human hair.

	The key was not to lose Skarsgård under the makeup. Dunckley says the team used 3D animation software: “We could track the expressive range of the face so that we could engineer into the weave the ability to move for his expression.”

	In all, it took under two hours to transform Skarsgård into the wicker husband. “90 minutes is where we were by the end of it,” Rubano says.

	Dunckley adds, “The other big piece to the puzzle was Alexander himself. What a wonderful collaborator and team player! He was resilient. He was funny. He was so invested. He would sit as still as a statue in the chair.”

	They encountered one small issue. Rubano reveals, “He runs hot; the suit’s kind of hot and it was a hot Hungarian spring.”
	

	And what about the wicker penis?

	“There’s been a lot of speculation about just the mechanics of how this would work and about the potential danger of a wicker penis,” Dunckley says. “I think the basket maker, he’s skilled. He’s traveled the world. He’s learned from every culture how to weave, and I think he would know exactly how to weave a wicker ween so it’s user-friendly.”

	Rubano credits the film’s costume designers András Dániel Tóth and Attila Godena-Juhász for that detail. “They fabricated the wicker ween for the full-body river shot. They did such a great job because it was very last minute, but it’s puff spandex. The weave was 3D, so there was dimension to it. From a distance, they color-matched it so beautifully.”

title: Blumhouse Soliciting Testimony from Anyone Who Feels ‘Personally Victimized’ by One of Its Movies or TV Shows
description:
Have any Blumhouse horror films scared the living shit out of you? The studio admits that you might have a case.

	But before you file that class a
body:
Have any Blumhouse horror films scared the living shit out of you? The studio admits that you might have a case.

	But before you file that class action lawsuit, Blumhouse is acting a bit tongue-in-cheek. To promote the new season of its USA Network legal thriller “The Rainmaker,” Blumhouse is putting out an ad calling on viewers who have been “personally victimized by a Blumhouse movie or series” and suggesting that “you may be entitled to compensation.”
	

	Emphasis on the “may.” In the fine print, Blumhouse adds: “No real lawsuit is being filed. No real legal claims are being made. Your trauma, however, is completely valid and we are prepared to argue that in front of absolutely no one.”


	But Blumhouse is indeed looking for those who feel they’ve been wrongfully spooked to file their complaints at bit.ly/blumhouseclaims, and the studio will collect and share those submissions on its social accounts.

	The spoof ad was launched Friday on Blumhouse’s social channels as well as through the Blumhouse Atomic Monster newsletter “The Van.”

	“’The Rainmaker’ is every bit a Blumhouse show, and we wanted to celebrate it in a way that felt true to who we are,” said Blumhouse Atomic Monster chief marketing officer Karen Barragan. “So this idea is about bridging those worlds, speaking to the existing fandom and expanding the audience. We had to have many, many discussions with lawyers as you can imagine, but it was worth it and we love the result.”

	The campaign comes as Season 2 gets underway, with Episode 2 airing this Friday on USA Network. The series is also now available on Prime Video, where it was No. 9 across all content in the U.S. on Friday.
	

	Season 1 of “The Rainmaker” was also USA Network’s most-watched freshman series in seven years was the most-watched new scripted TV series across cable in 2025.

	Here’s this season’s logline: “Rudy Baylor (played by Milo Callaghan), an underdog lawyer takes on powerful interests alongside his boss Jocelyn “Bruiser” Stone (Lana Parrilla) and his right-hand man Deck Shifflet (P.J. Byrne), the firm’s colorful paralegal. This season, J. Lyman Stone and Associates faces old adversaries and new ones in a case where the lives of hundreds of children hang in the balance, and where winning might be just as dangerous as losing. Later, Rudy goes up against his former law school flame, Sarah Plankmore (Madison Iseman), in the courtroom at the behest of her mysterious new boss, Amanda Vonn (Merle Dandridge), a powerful attorney whose agenda may be hiding a shocking international conspiracy. In a separate case, Bruiser’s ex-husband Tom Cassady (Austin Nichols) turns to her for help as his legal troubles threaten his life and that of the star pitcher (Liam O’Halloran) of the minor league baseball team he coaches.”

	Quipped “The Rainmaker” exec producer/showrunner Michael Seitzman: “I ran it past Rudy, Deck and Bruiser. They took one look at the box office for ‘Obsession’ and said, that’s our whale.”

	Lionsgate Television and Blumhouse Atomic Monster are behind the show. Michael Seitzman is showrunner and exec producer; John Grisham, Patrick Moran, Jason Richman, David Gernert and Jason Blum are also executive producers.

            Letitia James is pushing back on claims that she's biased against the Cornell 7 ... telling a judge she posted about the alleged victim out of empathy -- but she still can investigate without any prejudice against the accused men.
      
    
            The New York Attorney General filed a letter along with NY Governor Kathy Hochul, in response to an ethics complaint filed against her.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Gillio Lopes -- one of the people accused in Jane Doe's lawsuit -- filed docs trying to get her dismissed from the investigation and replaced with someone else ... but James claims she was just expressing empathy ... not actually supporting the alleged victim -- and she also says that Lopes has no standing to question her appointment because he hasn't even been charged with a crime and it's entirely speculative that he ever will.
      

            James and Hochul also say Hochul's decision to appoint James falls under the governor's broad discretion ... and generally can't be second-guessed.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A hearing on the matter is scheduled for October 29.
      
    
            As you know ... James' office is looking into the latter to determine if criminal charges should be filed against any of the Cornell frat brothers over the allegations by Jane Doe.

            One of the women suing Nick Carter for sexual assault claims she confided in actress Kaley Cuoco days after the alleged incident ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            TMZ obtained the transcript of accuser Melissa Schuman's deposition in April, and it reveals the former Dream singer was grilled about who she told about the alleged assault.
      
    
            Remember ... Melissa claims Nick assaulted her inside a Santa Monica apartment around 2003 ... when she was 18, and Nick was 22.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            During the deposition, Melissa testified she confided in Kaley on the final day of filming in April 2003 ... Kaley and Melissa starred in a film, "The Hollows," released in 2004 … along with Nick.
      

            Melissa also testified that she received a text from Nick after returning to the set and claims he called her and told her she was a "manipulative bitch."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Melissa and another woman named Shannon Ruth sued Nick over separate alleged sexual assaults. Melissa filed a police report in 2017, but no criminal charges were ever filed.
      
    
            Nick adamantly denies the allegations, and is countersuing ... claiming the women conspired to shake him down.
      
    
            Nick claims Melissa cost him millions in business and endorsement deals.
      
    
            In his lawsuit, the Backstreet Boys star describes the night in question as consensual. His suit says, "After having consensual sex, [Melissa] and [Nick] fell asleep. [Melissa] slept next to [Nick] through the night."
      
    
            The lawsuit adds, "At no point in time did [Nick] sexually assault [Melissa] or any other person."
      
    
            Both cases are ongoing.
